A1.justification: Both PDFs describe LongAlign. Their complete main texts, equations, figures, tables, and appendices are readable, and retained material can be matched across relocation and renumbering.

before.justification: v1 reports original retrieval and image-generation experiments, encoding and reward-reweighting ablations, and GPT-4o evaluations in Section 5 and the appendices.

after.justification: v2 retains those original results and adds segmentation analyses, DPG-Bench and prompt-length evaluations, and SDXL experiments.

M1.justification: Segment encoding, special-token handling, preference decomposition, gradient reweighting, the selected preference loss in Appendix B.1, and Algorithm 1 are retained. The SDXL experiments apply the existing method without documenting a new procedure.

E1.justification: Appendix C.3 adds DPG-Bench compositional generation coverage and generation evaluations spanning short prompts through approximately 500-token GPT-4o-generated prompts. These extend the original generation evaluation beyond its retained caption dataset; the earlier sentence-length experiment evaluated retrieval.

E2.justification: ELLA becomes an evaluated comparator in Table 2, having previously only been cited. Appendix C.4 also adds an SDXL versus longSDXL comparison. Existing foundation-model, preference-model, and P2I comparators are retained.

E3.justification: v2 adds VQAscore, DPG-Bench evaluation, controlled prompt-length conditions at 15, 60, 120, 240, and approximately 500 tokens, and SDXL generation at 1024 × 1024. Appendix C.3 specifies sentence-boundary truncation and evaluation against the entire supplied prompt despite baseline input limits. Previously stated training and sampling settings remain unchanged.

E4.justification: New analyses test retaining one versus all start tokens, grouping multiple sentences per segment, cross-sentence attention behavior, and retrieval under the two existing preference losses. Appendix C also adds qualitative reweighting comparisons and generation sensitivity to prompt length. These extend the original token-removal, encoding, and reward-weight ablations.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental seed counts, repeated-run uncertainty, confidence intervals, or significance tests. The retained score-distribution histograms describe embedding scores rather than uncertainty across experimental runs.

E6.justification: Original benchmark entries are retained, while v2 adds VQAscore, ELLA, DPG-Bench, prompt-length, SDXL, and qualitative results. DPG-Bench reports 77.58 for longSD versus 74.91 for ELLA1.5. The new SDXL comparison raises Denscore-O from 33.52 to 37.33 but worsens FID from 21.18 to 23.88. Table 10 also reports SD1.5 Denscore-O as 29.29, inconsistent with 29.20 retained in Table 2.

T1.justification: Equation 6 and the following average-score and embedding definitions correct summation bounds from k=i to k=1; the score identity also corrects an inconsistent image argument. This repairs the mathematical expressions to match averaging all segments, already reflected in v1's appendix losses. No new theorem or proof is introduced.

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution bullets, and main conclusion retain the claims about segment-level encoding, decomposed preference optimization, reduced overfitting, and fine-tuned SD1.5 outperforming stronger models in long-text alignment. The additional experiments support these existing claims.

C2.justification: Section 7 replaces the specific entity-count limitation with difficulties involving complex contextual dependencies and strong semantic understanding. Appendix A adds an interpretation of cross-attention examples as evidence of cross-sentence handling, while Appendix C.4 discusses stronger foundation models and their smaller relative improvements.

D1.justification: v2 documents prompt-length construction, discarding incomplete sentences, the GPT-4o origin of approximately 500-token prompts, and full prompts for the new SDXL examples. Original training hyperparameters, hardware disclosures, pseudocode, GPT-4o evaluation code, and code-access information remain unchanged.

R1.justification: v2 adds references to Lin et al. (2024) for VQAscore and Podell et al. (2023) for SDXL. ELLA, already cited in v1, gains an explicit experimental comparison role. The related-work section and overall research positioning remain substantially unchanged.

P1.justification: The main narrative is largely retained, with localized wording corrections and expanded explanations. v2 adds acknowledgments and an ethics statement, updates publication and author information, and organizes Appendix C into subsections. The additions do not amount to extensive rewriting of the existing paper.

P2.justification: v2 adds substantial visual material: Figures 11–13 and 17, benchmark tables, and SDXL image-comparison tables. Table 2 gains an ELLA column and VQAscore row. The original P2I table moves unchanged from main-text Table 3 to Appendix D, Table 11; existing appendix figures are retained and renumbered.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens validation of the unchanged method. Beyond v1's custom-dataset results and GPT-4o checks, it adds a standardized compositional benchmark, complementary alignment metric, controlled prompt-length evaluations, SDXL transfer, and targeted segmentation analyses. These address important gaps in evidence for generalization and design choices. The SDXL FID regression, absent run uncertainty, and numerical inconsistency temper the conclusions, but do not outweigh the stronger empirical support.
